findings.quote: One of the reasons why Evans introduces the variable "brilliance" is the observation that colored stimuli that are equal in luminance are usually not equally bright.
He points out that some experts are able to make brightness matches that are also equal in luminance.
These experts, ostensibly, ignore the variable he calls brilliance.

findings.antecedent: Direct heterochromatic brightness matching vs. flicker photometry
findings.quote: A number of investigators during the last ten years have studied this discrepancy and come to the conclusion that the basic difference between brightness and luminance rests in the different methodologies underlying these measures.

findings.antecedent: More-saturated spectral lights (adjusted to equal luminance)
findings.quote: In my own color lexicon, I see the more-saturated spectral lights as brighter than less-saturated lights when all are adjusted to equal luminance.

findings.antecedent: Stimuli equated for luminance (during flicker photometry)
findings.quote: When various stimuli are equated for luminance, I assume that they are equated for achromatic activity because, during flicker photometry, only the achromatic part of the visual system enters into the minimum-flicker judgment.
But when stimuli are not being flickered, we perceive the brightness associated with the achromatic visual activity and also the chromatic visual activity.
The chromatic visual activity conveys hue and brightness information, whereas the achromatic visual system carries brightness and whiteness information.
The chromatic visual activity conveys hue and brightness information, whereas the achromatic visual system carries brightness and whiteness information.

findings.consequent: Similarity to saturation-discrimination curves, equivalent contrast of chromatic stimulus, ratio of brightness-matching luminous-efficiency function to flicker photometry function, and magnitude estimates of white content of spectral stimuli
findings.quote: As Evans noted, G_phi functions are similar to saturation-discrimination curves. They are also similar to curves that represent the equivalent contrast of a chromatic stimulus set for minimally distinct border with a precisely juxtaposed white stimulus. A similar function is obtained as the ratio of a brightness-matching luminous-efficiency function to a similar function obtained when the same observer uses flicker photometry. Curves that have similar shapes are also obtained from magnitude estimates of the white content of spectral stimuli.
Evans makes the astounding statement that-"...aside perhaps from yellow, no achromatic component at all is usually perceived in a pure spectrum." (page 120).
Jacobs found that different amounts of achromatic content were reported as a function of wavelength.
Evans asserts that "to assume instead that the various monochromatic stimuli differ in chromatic strength, that is, brilliance, accords far more nearly with what is actually seen." (page 120).
He suggested to Selig Hecht the possibility that color vision is mediated by cones and rods.
At that meeting, there were several papers reporting data on rod-cone interactions and their relationship to color vision.
Evans repeatedly suggests the use of "inter-eye comparisons," suggesting that that is the only way that adequate data on color perception can be obtained.
